problem: Prior character animation and visual navigation work either assumes privileged 3D scene knowledge (producing optimal but unnatural search) or relies on random exploration and fixed heads; end-to-end visuomotor learning with full-body characters in photorealistic scenes is too costly.
motivation: Searching for objects is an everyday behavior. Depriving the character of privileged information and forcing it to rely on egocentric RGBD-like vision should yield human-like coordinated look-around and locomotion. Decoupling search from full-body motion makes training tractable and lets one policy be reused across characters.
key_idea: Train an agent-agnostic vision-based search policy (SAC+CURL) on an abstract cylinder-plus-independent-head model, then transfer it zero-shot to full-body humanoid and robot characters through MPC-like online replanning with a motion generator.
insight: Allowing independent head movement gives about 20% higher success than a body-only-rotation baseline (training curves), showing active gaze is crucial for search. Long-horizon replanning matters: a 1-step baseline and random-noise exploration are each about 40% worse in SPL, and smaller replanning interval M gives higher SPL at more compute. Camera height randomization is what enables transfer, and height trades off which surfaces are visible: 1.05m and 1.65m score 92% and 90% excluding cabinets, versus 50% for 0.45m.
method: Abstract model: cylinder body plus 2-DoF camera head, with observations of depth 84x84 (5 m max, 90° FOV, K=5 history), a target-mask feature vector (centroid, polar coords, 5x5 downsampled mask) and head pitch/yaw; no RGB and no global pose.
Action space: relative [Δx, Δy, Δθ, Δq_pitch, Δq_yaw] tracked by position control in PyBullet.

Reward: success +10, negative distance to the goal when visible, live penalty -0.1, and collision penalty clipped to [-3,0]; weights [1,1,1,0.1]; max 100 steps; success within 0.5 m with the target visible.

Training: SAC with CURL contrastive representation learning, Pixel CNN encoder to 128-d, 3 FC layers of 1024, 0.75M samples; domain randomization of body height in [1.0,1.8] m and ±0.1 m vertical noise.
Online replanning motion synthesis: roll out the policy for T steps in the abstract model, feed the trajectory to PFNN or NSM to get full-body poses, and keep only the first M steps.
Memory repair: regenerate the depth history and head orientations from the full-body root poses for the M executed steps, then replan.
Transfer: the same policy is applied to a human (1.65 m, via PFNN or NSM) and directly to a Fetch differential-drive robot (1.05 m).

setting.backbone: Pixel CNN encoder + MLP actor/critic trained from scratch with SAC+CURL; PFNN/NSM motion generators (pretrained, from prior work)
setting.training_data: Online RL in iGibson, 0.75M simulation samples in a single home scene with randomized start and object positions
setting.observation: egocentric depth (84x84) + target segmentation mask feature + head joint angles; no RGB, no global pose
setting.action_space: continuous relative body motion (Δx, Δy, Δyaw) plus independent camera pitch/yaw deltas, realized by kinematic motion generators
setting.privileged: Target object segmentation mask given as input; 3D info used only for the training reward; the test scene is the same home as in training

numbers.eval_set_note: 100 random scenarios, abstract model, excluding low floor cabinets, head height 1.65m
100 random scenarios, objects sampled everywhere including low cabinets, 1.65m

numbers_note: The success-rate figures are in Table 1 only. The SPL and number-of-attempts comparisons (1-step, noisy search, different M) and the head-vs-no-head training curves appear only in figures (text says ~40% higher SPL than 1-step and noisy search, ~20% higher success with head movement), so they are not tabulated. The benchmark is the authors' own custom scene, not a standard one.
results: The abstract search policy reaches about 90-92% success for 1.05-1.65 m camera heights when low cabinets are excluded (75-76% with them), versus 50% for 0.45 m. The head-movement ablation gives about 20% higher success, and the full method is about 40% better in SPL than the 1-step and noisy-search baselines. The same policy transfers zero-shot to PFNN/NSM humanoids and a Fetch robot.
limitations: Relies on a given target-object segmentation mask, has only a 5-step depth memory, and was tested in a single home scene, so it does not scale to whole buildings or unseen scenes.
Collision checking is done only on the abstract cylinder, so the full-body character sometimes penetrates furniture; replanning with small M is computationally costly.
Assumes small height variation during locomotion and no interaction (e.g., opening drawers).
